sources.excerpt:
This feature is well established and works across many devices and browser versions. Itâs been available across browsers since July 2015.

The GET HTTP method requests a representation of the specified resource.

Requests using GET should only be used to request data and shouldn't contain a body.

The semantics of sending a message body in GET requests are undefined.

Some servers may reject the request with a 4XX client error response.

GET <request-target>["?"<query>] HTTP/1.1

- Identifies the target resource of the request when combined with the information provided in the Host header.

This is an absolute path (e.g., /path/to/file.html) in requests to an origin server, and an absolute URL in requests to proxies (e.g., http://www.example.com/path/to/file.html).

- An optional query component preceded by a question-mark ?.

Often used to carry identifying information in the form of key=value pairs.

The server sends back the resource with a 200 OK status code, indicating success:

sources.title: HTTP request methods - MDN Web Docs
sources.excerpt:
HTTP defines a set of request methods to indicate the purpose of the request and what is expected if the request is successful. Although they can also be nouns, these request methods are sometimes referred to as HTTP verbs. Each request method has its own semantics, but some characteristics are shared across multiple methods, specifically request methods can be safe, idempotent, or cacheable.

- The GET method requests a representation of the specified resource.

Requests using GET should only retrieve data and should not contain a request content.

- The QUERY method initiates a server-side query. It requests that the target resource process the request content in a safe and idempotent manner, returning the result in the response.

It is similar to GET, but allows request content with defined semantics.

- The HEAD method asks for a response identical to a GET request, but without a response body.

- The POST method submits an entity to the specified resource, often causing a change in state or side effects on the server.

- The PUT method replaces all current representations of the target resource with the request content.

- The DELETE method deletes the specified resource.

- The CONNECT method establishes a tunnel to the server identified by the target resource.

- The OPTIONS method describes the communication options for the target resource.

- The TRACE method performs a message loop-back test along the path to the target resource.

- The PATCH method applies partial modifications to a resource.

Safe, idempotent, and cacheable request methods

The following table lists HTTP request methods and their categorization in terms of safety, cacheability, and idempotency.

| Method | Safe | Idempotent | Cacheable |

* POST and PATCH are cacheable when responses explicitly include freshness information and a matching Content-Location header.

sources.title: HTTP: Hypertext Transfer Protocol | MDN - MDN Web Docs
sources.excerpt:
HTTP follows a classical client-server model, with a client opening a connection to make a request, then waiting until it receives a response from the server. HTTP is a stateless protocol, meaning that the server does not keep any session data between two requests, although the later addition of cookies adds state to some client-server interactions.

HTTP is an extensible protocol that relies on concepts like resources and Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs), a basic message structure, and client-server communication model. On top of these concepts, numerous extensions have been developed over the years that add functionality and updated semantics, including additional HTTP methods and headers.

- HTTP was created in the early 1990s and has been extended several times. This article goes through its history and describes HTTP/0.9, HTTP/1.0, HTTP/1.1, through HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, as well as novelties introduced over the years.

- HTTP messages transmitted as requests and responses have a defined structure. This article describes this general structure, its purpose, and the different types of messages.

- A range request asks the server to send a specific part (or parts) of a resource back to a client instead of the full resource. Range requests are useful for cases when a client knows they need only part of a large file, or for cases where an application allows the user to pause and resume a download.

- Client Hints are a set of response headers that a server can use to proactively request information from a client about the device, network, user, and user-agent-specific preferences. The server can then determine which resources to send, based on the information that the client chooses to provide.

- Cross-site HTTP requests are requests for resources from a different domain than that of the resource making the request.

The HTTP reference documentation contains detailed information about headers, request methods, status responses, and lists relevant specifications and standards documents.

- Request methods indicate the purpose of the request and what is expected if the request is successful.

- Response status codes indicate the outcome of a specific HTTP request. Responses are grouped in five classes: informational, successful, redirections, client errors, and server errors.

In HTTP/2 and above, headers are displayed in lowercase when viewed in developer tools (accept: */*), and prefixed with a colon for a special group of pseudo-headers (:status: 200).

Designed with extensibility in mind, it has seen numerous additions over the years; this led to its specification being scattered through numerous specification documents (in the midst of experimental abandoned extensions). sources.title: List of HTTP status codes - Wikipedia
sources.excerpt:
- The server has received the request headers and the client should proceed to send the request body (in the case of a request for which a body needs to be sent, such as a POST request). Sending a large request body to a server after a request has been rejected for inappropriate headers would be inefficient. To have a server check the request's headers, a client must send Expect: 100-continue as a header in its initial request and receive a 100 Continue status code in response before sending the body. If the client receives an error code such as 403 (Forbidden) or 405 (Method Not Allowed) then it should not send the request's body. The response 417 Expectation Failed indicates that the request should be repeated without the Expect header as it indicates that the server does not support expectations (this is the case, for example, of HTTP/1.0 servers).[2]: §10.1.1

- A WebDAV request may contain many sub-requests involving file operations, requiring a long time to complete the request. This code indicates that the server has received and is processing the request, but no response is available yet.[3] This prevents the client from timing out and assuming the request was lost. The status code is deprecated.[4]

- Standard response for successful HTTP requests. The actual response will depend on the request method used. In a GET request, the response will contain an entity corresponding to the requested resource. In a POST request, the response will contain an entity describing or containing the result of the action.

- The link target was moved such that the request and future similar requests should be redirected to the given URI. If a client has link-editing capabilities, it should update references to the request URL. The response is cacheable unless indicated otherwise. Except for a GET request, the body should contain a hyperlink to the new URL(s). Except for a GET or HEAD request, the client must ask the user before redirecting.[9]This code is considered best practice for upgrading users from HTTP to HTTPS. Both Bing and Google recommend using this code to change the URL of a page as it is shown in search engine results, providing that URL will permanently change and is not due to be changed again any time soon.[10][11]

sources.title: HTTP - Wikipedia
sources.excerpt:
Data is exchanged through a sequence of request–response messages which are exchanged by a session layer transport connection. An HTTP client initially tries to establish a connection, real or virtual, with a server. An HTTP server listening on the port accepts the connection and then waits for a client's request message. The client sends its HTTP request message. Upon receiving the request the server sends back an HTTP response message, which includes header(s) plus a body if it is required. The body of this response message is typically the requested resource, although an error message or other information may also be returned. At any time and for many reasons, either the client or server can close the connection. Closing a connection is usually advertised by one or more HTTP headers in the last request or response.

HTTP/1.1 added also HTTP pipelining in order to further reduce lag time when using persistent connections by allowing clients to send multiple requests before waiting for each response.  This optimization was never considered really safe because a few web servers and many proxy servers, specially transparent proxy servers placed in Internet / Intranets between clients and servers, did not handle pipelined requests properly (they served only the first request discarding the others, they closed the connection because they saw more data after the first request or some proxies even returned responses out of order etc.).  Because of this, only HEAD and some GET requests (i.e. limited to real file requests and so with URLs without query string used as a command, etc.) could be pipelined in a safe and idempotent mode.  After many years of struggling with the problems introduced by enabling pipelining, this feature was first disabled and then removed from most browsers. Pipelining was also removed because of the announced adoption of HTTP/2.

In 2014, HTTP/0.9 was deprecated for servers supporting version HTTP/1.1 (and higher):Since HTTP/0.9 did not support header fields in a request, there is no mechanism for it to support name-based virtual hosts (selection of resource by inspection of the Host header field).  Any server that implements name-based virtual hosts ought to disable support for HTTP/0.9.  Most requests that appear to be HTTP/0.9 are, in fact, badly constructed HTTP/1.x requests caused by a client failing to properly encode the request-target.

sources.title: HTTP GET Method: Complete Guide with Examples
sources.excerpt:
TL;DR: GET fetches whatever lives at a URL: a page, an image, a JSON record. It should never change server state, which is why browsers, crawlers, and caches feel free to repeat and prefetch it. Put parameters in the query string, not a body. Responses are cacheable when the status and Cache-Control headers allow it.

GET responses are cacheable, though not every one gets stored. Cache-Control: no-store keeps a response out of caches; no-cache lets caches store it but makes them revalidate before each reuse. Freshness is measured against the responseâs age, which includes time spent in upstream caches, not just time since your browser received it. See HTTP caching.

Accept says which media type the client wants; Content-Type says what it got. ETag identifies a version for conditional requests. Vary: Accept-Encoding tells caches that the response depends on that request header. Bearer tokens go in Authorization, not a query parameter.

GET reads. POST asks the server to process what you send, however that resource defines it. POST can carry a large search document that wonât fit comfortably in a query string, but its responses are much harder to cache. Neither method encrypts anything; thatâs HTTPSâs job.

Thereâs no universal 2,000-character URL limit. Each hop sets its own. For example, nginx requires a request line to fit in one large_client_header_buffers buffer and returns 414 otherwise; its documented default is 4 8k. Four 8k buffers still mean a single request line has to fit in 8k, not 32k.

Open the GET playground preset, change the query, and watch the request URL change. When debugging caching on your own server, compare the first responseâs ETag with the validator sent on the next request.

GET retrieves a representation; POST submits content for resource-specific processing. GET responses are cacheable under HTTP cache rules. POST responses can also be cached with explicit freshness and a Content-Location matching the target URI.

sections.title: Why does a web page sometimes disappear after you click a button?
sections.content_md: Imagine you built a form that saves a new blog post. When you press **Submit**, the page either shows the new post or shows an error like *404 Not Found*. Which part of the HTTP conversation decides what you see?  In the next 45 minutes you’ll learn how the request method you choose (GET vs POST) and the server’s status code shape that experience.

sections.title: GET vs POST: What they are and when to use them
sections.content_md:
### GET
- Retrieves a representation of a resource without a request body. It is **safe** (doesn’t change server state) and **idempotent** – repeating the request has the same effect [S1][S2].
- Parameters are placed in the query string: `GET /search?q=books HTTP/1.1` [S1].
- Ideal for reading data, bookmarking, and caching.

### POST
- Sends data to the server in the request body (e.g., form fields, JSON). Not safe and not idempotent – each call can create a new resource [S2].
- Used for creating resources, submitting forms, or any operation that changes state.
- Example request line: `POST /api/articles HTTP/1.1` with `Content-Type: application/json` header.

### Safe vs Idempotent
| Property | GET | POST |
|----------|-----|------|
| Safe? | ✅ | ❌ |
| Idempotent? | ✅ | ❌ |
| Typical use‑case | Read‑only fetches, search queries | Create/update actions, file uploads |

**Headers that matter**
- `Accept` tells the server which media types you can handle.
- `Content-Type` describes the media type of a message body. You send it whenever your request has a body (POST, PUT, PATCH), and servers also send it on responses.
- `Host` and the request line together identify the target resource [S4].

sections.title: Response status code families
sections.content_md:
HTTP responses start with a three‑digit status code. The first digit groups them:

| Family | Meaning | Common codes |
|--------|---------|--------------|
| **2xx** | Success – the request was received, understood, and processed [S5]. | `200 OK`, `201 Created` |
| **4xx** | Client error – the request has bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled [S5]. | `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `404 Not Found` |
| **5xx** | Server error – the server failed to fulfill a valid request [S5]. | `500 Internal Server Error`, `503 Service Unavailable` |

**What the codes tell you**
- `200` means the GET succeeded and the body contains the requested data.
- `201` is returned after a successful POST that created a new resource.
- `400` indicates the client sent malformed data (e.g., missing required fields).
- `404` means the target URL does not exist.
- `500` signals a problem on the server side, not the client’s fault.

These families help you decide how to handle the response in code (retry, show error, etc.).

sections.title: Worked examples with curl
sections.content_md:
### Example 1 – GET request
```bash
curl -i "https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1"
```
Output (truncated):
```
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
{"userId":1,"id":1,"title":"..."}
```
- Status **200** → success (2xx family) [S5].
- No request body, only a query path [S1].

### Example 2 – POST request
```bash
curl -i -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \
     -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
     -d '{"title":"My Post","body":"Hello","userId":1}'
```
Output (truncated):
```
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...
{"id":101,"title":"My Post","body":"Hello","userId":1}
```
- Status **201** → resource created (2xx family) [S5].
- Request includes a JSON body and `Content-Type` header.

### Example 3 – Client error (4xx)
JSONPlaceholder is a *fake* API: it accepts any body and does not validate input, so you can't trigger a 400 there.
Ask for a resource that doesn't exist instead:
```bash
curl -i https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/99999
```
Response:
```
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
```
Shows how the server signals client‑side problems [S5].

sections.title: Hands‑on: Make GET and POST calls and interpret status codes
sections.content_md:
#### Goal
Use **curl** (or any HTTP client) to send GET and POST requests to a public test API and record the status codes.

#### Steps
1. Open a terminal.
2. **GET** a known resource:
   ```bash
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/5
   ```
   *Write down the code you see.*
3. **POST** a new resource:
   ```bash
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \
        -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d '{"title":"Test","body":"Demo","userId":1}'
   ```
   *Note the code.*
4. **Trigger a client error** by requesting a non‑existent endpoint:
   ```bash
   curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/unknown
   ```
5. **Trigger a server error** (optional): `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://httpbin.org/status/500` (httpbin returns whatever status code you ask for).
6. Fill the table below:

| Request | URL | Method | Status code | Family |
|---------|-----|--------|-------------|--------|
| 1 | … | GET | … | … |
| 2 | … | POST | … | … |
| 3 | … | GET | … | … |
| 4 | … | GET | … | … |

#### Expected outcome
- GET returns **200** (2xx).
- POST returns **201** (2xx).
- Bad URL returns **404** (4xx).
- Optional server error returns **500** (5xx).
- Map each code to its family and explain why it occurred.

sections.title: Quiz – Test your understanding
sections.content_md:
1. **Which HTTP method is safe and idempotent?**
   - A) GET  **(Correct)**
   - B) POST
   - C) DELETE
2. **When should you use POST instead of GET?**
   - A) To retrieve a cached image
   - B) To submit form data that creates a new record **(Correct)**
   - C) To bookmark a page
3. **What does a 404 status code indicate?**
   - A) Server malfunction
   - B) Client requested a non‑existent resource **(Correct)**
   - C) Request succeeded
4. **Which family does 503 belong to and what does it mean?**
   - A) 2xx – Success
   - B) 4xx – Client error
   - C) 5xx – Server error, service unavailable **(Correct)**
5. **A POST request receives a 201 response. What should you infer?**
   - A) The request failed
   - B) A new resource was created successfully **(Correct)**
   - C) The client sent bad data

**Answer key**
1. GET is defined as safe and idempotent[S1].
2. POST is used for actions that change server state[S5].
3. 404 signals the target URL does not exist[S5].
4. 5xx codes indicate server‑side problems; 503 means service unavailable[S5].
5. 201 means the server created a resource as a result of the POST[S5].

sections.title: Key takeaways & common pitfalls
sections.content_md:
### Remember
- **GET** = read‑only, safe, idempotent, query string for parameters.
- **POST** = send data, changes state, not safe nor idempotent.
- Status families: **2xx** success, **4xx** client error, **5xx** server error.
- Common codes: 200, 201, 400, 401, 404, 500, 503.

### Common mistakes
- Putting a request body in a GET – many servers will reject it with a 4xx [S1].
- Ignoring the response code and assuming success.
- Forgetting to set `Content-Type` for POST bodies, leading to 400 errors.

Use the status code to decide whether to retry, show a user‑friendly error, or proceed.

claims.claim: POST is used for creating resources, submitting forms, or any operation that changes state
claims.note: MDN describes POST for state-changing operations

claims.claim: Content-Type header is sent whenever the request has a body (POST, PUT, PATCH)
Host header together with request line identifies the target resource
claims.note: MDN reference mentions Host header role

claims.claim: 2xx status codes indicate success – request was received, understood, and processed
4xx status codes indicate client error – bad syntax or cannot be fulfilled
5xx status codes indicate server error – server failed to fulfill a valid request
200 OK means GET succeeded and body contains requested data
201 Created is returned after a successful POST that created a new resource
400 Bad Request indicates client sent malformed data (e.g., missing required fields)
404 Not Found means target URL does not exist
500 Internal Server Error signals a problem on the server side, not the client’s fault
503 Service Unavailable is a 5xx server error indicating service unavailable
GET request to https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1 returns 200 OK
POST request to https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts returns 201 Created
GET request to https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/99999 returns 404 Not Found
GET is safe and idempotent
POST is used for actions that change server state
404 indicates client requested a non-existent resource
503 belongs to 5xx family and means service unavailable
201 response to POST means a new resource was created successfully

qc_instructional.summary: The lesson aligns well with the objectives, offers clear explanations, solid examples, and practical application. Minor adjustments to quiz wording, example breadth, and timing would enhance clarity and learner confidence.

issues.description: Quiz question 3 asks about 404 but answer key incorrectly cites 404 as client error; the explanation in the key is correct but the question wording could mislead learners into thinking 404 is a server error.
issues.evidence: Question 3: "What does a 404 status code indicate?" – answer key says client requested a non‑existent resource.
issues.suggestion: Rephrase answer key to explicitly state 404 is a client error and add a brief note in the question to avoid confusion.

issues.description: Worked examples rely on a fake API that does not allow triggering 400 errors, limiting the demonstration of client‑error handling.
issues.evidence: Example 3 notes that JSONPlaceholder cannot trigger 400.
issues.suggestion: Include a second example using httpbin.org/status/400 to show a real 400 response, or explain why 400 cannot be demonstrated with the chosen API.

issues.description: Hook uses a scenario but could be more interactive by asking learners to predict the outcome before revealing the explanation.
issues.suggestion: Add a quick poll or a prompt: "What do you think will happen when you click Submit?" to increase engagement.

issues.description: The table of safe vs idempotent properties uses check marks that may not be accessible to all learners; also the term "idempotent" is not defined in plain language.
issues.evidence: Table under "Safe vs Idempotent" uses ✅/❌ symbols.
issues.suggestion: Add a brief definition of idempotent (e.g., "repeating the request has the same effect") and replace symbols with text for clarity.

issues.description: Quiz question 5 asks learners to infer from a 201 response but does not explicitly connect it to the earlier explanation of POST creating resources.
issues.evidence: Question 5: "A POST request receives a 201 response. What should you infer?"
issues.suggestion: Add a short explanatory note in the quiz or in the lesson that 201 indicates a resource was created to reinforce the link.

issues.description: The activity allocates 9 minutes but includes five curl commands plus a table to fill; this may be tight for beginners.
issues.suggestion: Provide a pre‑filled example table and reduce the number of curl commands to two (GET and POST) to fit the time budget.

objective_coverage.component: Explain GET and POST methods, their characteristics (safe, idempotent) and typical use‑cases
